content: Based on the findings that muscle power and explosive strength are closely linked to functional performance in older adults, it has been proposed that resistance training performed at fast, intentional velocities may lead to greater improvements in functional capacity compared to moderate-velocity resistance training. However, there is currently no high-quality systematic review or meta-analysis to substantiate this claim. A recent study compared the extent of functional capacity improvements between fast-intentional velocity and moderate-velocity resistance training. Databases such as PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched up to January 2019. When multiple functional tests were used in a study, a single pooled standardized mean difference was calculated to represent combined functional capacity. Functional tests were also grouped based on their specificity for subgroup meta-analyses. Fifteen studies were selected, including three high-quality studies and two pre-registered studies. The results suggest inconclusive evidence to support the superiority of fast-intentional velocity resistance training over moderate-velocity resistance training in improving functional capacity. These findings may have been influenced by the limited number of high-quality and pre-registered studies, high heterogeneity, and small-study publication bias. Another systematic review and meta-analysis examined the association of long-term exercise interventions (lasting one year or more) with the risk of falls, fractures, hospitalizations, and mortality in older adults. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with participants aged 60 years or older. Data were extracted and synthesized using risk ratios (RRs) and random-effects models. The results showed that long-term exercise was associated with a reduction in falls, injurious falls, and possibly fractures in older adults, including those with cardiometabolic and neurological diseases. However, exercise did not significantly reduce the risk of multiple falls, hospitalizations, or mortality. Meta-regressions suggested that exercising two to three times per week may be the optimal frequency for these benefits. A systematic review of exercise-based fall prevention strategies in adults aged 50 years or older with visual impairment found that while exercise can improve physical function, there are no proven strategies for preventing falls in this population. The review highlighted the need for more research to investigate falls prevention in older adults with visual impairment. Another meta-analysis evaluated the effects of wearable sensor-based balance and gait training on balance, gait, and functional performance in both healthy and patient populations. The review included eight RCTs and found positive effects of wearable sensor training on static balance and specific gait parameters. However, the evidence was limited by small sample sizes, short intervention durations, and heterogeneous training paradigms. Larger studies are needed to better estimate the potential of wearable sensor technology. A meta-analysis on the effects of exercise alone or combined with dietary supplements in older adults with sarcopenic obesity found that both interventions improved muscle-related outcomes and reduced fat-related outcomes. However, better-designed RCTs are needed to systematically assess the effects of different exercise regimens and dietary supplements in this population. A systematic review on the association between social networks and long-term health risk behaviors found that individuals with smaller social networks had persistently unhealthy risk factor profiles over two decades. These associations were consistent across subgroups stratified by gender, age, and education. A systematic review of interventions to improve physical performance in pre-frail and frail older adults found that physical activity interventions significantly improved physical outcomes in these populations. A meta-analytical review of exercise training on handgrip strength in older adults found small but meaningful improvements in handgrip strength across various training approaches. However, handgrip strength may not be a reliable indicator of general functional performance for all exercise programs, and task-specific or multimodal training appears to be more effective. A systematic review and meta-analysis on the effects of free-living physical activity on balance in older adults found that physical activity improved balance outcomes, such as gait speed and functional reach, in healthy older adults. Finally, a Cochrane review on exercise for preventing falls in community-dwelling older adults found that exercise interventions targeting balance, gait, and muscle strength effectively reduced the rate of falls. However, most trials had unclear or high risk of bias, and further research is needed to refine exercise programs for fall prevention.
